formation.title: The Gujarat Sultanate
formation.text:
The banner of Gujarat flies over the lands between the Rann of Kutch and the Gulf of Khambat. For generations, the merchants of Cambay and Surat have enriched these shores with the wealth of the Indian Ocean, while the sultans have carved a kingdom from the contested borderlands of western India.

Now, as Gujarat stands united under a single crown, its ruler must decide what the sultanate shall become. Will it follow the path of Mahmud Begada, the Sultan of Land and Sea, building a military state that projects power across both its hinterland and the Arabian Sea? Or shall it embrace its destiny as the gateway of the Indian Ocean, a mercantile empire where trade and diplomacy are the instruments of greatness?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We shall be the Sultan of Land and Sea!

modifiers.name: Sultan of Land and Sea
modifiers.text: Following the example of Mahmud Begada, who styled himself Sultan al-Barr wa al-Bahr, Gujarat projects power across both its hinterland and the Arabian Sea.

options.text: Gujarat shall be the Gateway of the Indian Ocean.

modifiers.name: Gateway of the Indian Ocean
modifiers.text: Gujarat's ports stand at the crossroads of the world's richest trade routes, and its merchants have made themselves indispensable partners from East Africa to Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Stepwell Engineering
advances.text: The vav stepwells of Gujarat are among the most sophisticated water management structures in the medieval world, combining engineering prowess with sacred architecture.

advances.name: Muzaffarid Court
advances.text: The administrative traditions established by the Muzaffarid dynasty after independence from Delhi provide Gujarat with an efficient and stable governance system.

advances.name: Dhow Building Tradition
advances.text: Gujarat's shipwrights have perfected the construction of dhows: swift, lateen-rigged vessels ideally suited to the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean.

advances.name: Cambay Trade Network
advances.text: The port of Cambay has been a hub of international commerce for centuries, connecting Gujarat to the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and East Africa.

advances.name: Sultanate Tolerance
advances.text: The Gujarat Sultanate governs a diverse population of Muslims, Hindus, and Jains, maintaining social stability through pragmatic religious accommodation.

advances.name: Ghulam Military Tradition
advances.text: The ghulam system provides Gujarat's sultans with a corps of slave-soldier cavalry whose loyalty lies entirely with the throne rather than with any local nobleman.

advances.name: Habshi Palace Guard
advances.text: Abyssinian warriors, the Habshis, serve as elite palace guards and military commanders in the Gujarat Sultanate, prized for their martial skill and personal loyalty.

advances.name: Begada's Conquests
advances.text: Sultan Mahmud Begada earned his name, Lord of Two Forts, by conquering the seemingly impregnable strongholds of Champaner and Junagadh.

event.title: The Conquests of Mahmud Begada
event.text:
Sultan Mahmud Begada has earned his name, 'Lord of Two Forts', through the conquest of the seemingly impregnable fortresses of Champaner and Junagadh. The Rajput stronghold of Champaner, perched atop its rocky plateau, fell only after a prolonged and determined siege. Junagadh, seat of the Chudasama dynasty at the foot of sacred Mount Girnar, was brought to heel soon after.

These victories have transformed Gujarat from a coastal sultanate into a major power of western India. Yet Mahmud's ambitions extend beyond land. He has appointed Malik Ayyaz, a trusted commander of humble origin, as governor of Diu, where a formidable fleet is being assembled to secure Gujarat's maritime interests.

Will the Sultan continue to expand through conquest on land, or turn his gaze toward the sea?

options.text: The fortresses of India shall fall before us.

modifiers.name: Conqueror of Fortresses
modifiers.text: In the tradition of Mahmud Begada, who reduced the impregnable citadels of Champaner and Junagadh, Gujarat's armies specialize in the patient reduction of enemy strongholds.

options.text: Our destiny lies upon the waves.

modifiers.name: Lord of Diu
modifiers.text: Following Mahmud Begada's development of a powerful fleet off the coast of Diu, Gujarat commands the Arabian Sea approaches to the Indian subcontinent.

advances.name: Patola Silk Weaving
advances.text: The double-ikat Patola silk of Patan represents the most technically demanding textile art in India, producing fabrics treasured by royalty across the subcontinent.

advances.name: Champaner-Pavagadh
advances.text: The transformation of conquered Champaner into a magnificent capital city represents the golden age of Indo-Islamic architecture in western India.

event.title: The Glory of Champaner-Pavagadh
event.text:
Following the conquest of Champaner, Sultan Mahmud Begada has transformed the ancient hill fortress into a magnificent new capital. Where once stood only Rajput battlements, a city of mosques, palaces, and gardens is rising. The Jama Masjid of Champaner, with its soaring minarets and 172 intricately carved pillars, represents the pinnacle of Indo-Islamic architecture: a synthesis of Hindu structural traditions and Islamic decorative arts found nowhere else in India.

The Kevada Masjid, the Nagina Masjid, and the Shahar ki Masjid each display a different facet of this unique architectural tradition. The Mandvi customs house speaks to Gujarat's continuing commercial vitality, while the Citadel Jahanpanah proclaims the sultanate's military strength.

Champaner-Pavagadh stands as a monument to Gujarat's golden age.

advances.name: Bandhani Craft
advances.text:
The ancient Gujarati art of Bandhani, resist tie-dyeing, produces brilliantly colored textiles prized across the Indian Ocean world.

Available in: Karkhana Workshop

advances.name: Battle of Diu
advances.text: The clash between Gujarat's fleet and Portuguese warships off Diu in 1509 marked a turning point in Indian Ocean naval warfare and European expansion.

event.title: The Battle of Diu
event.text:
The waters off Diu have run red with blood. A great fleet assembled by the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, supported by Gujarat's own warships and ships from Calicut, has clashed with the Portuguese Estado da India. The outcome has demonstrated the terrible power of European heavy cannon at sea.

The Portuguese victory at Diu in 1509 has shaken the established order of Indian Ocean trade. For centuries, Gujarat's merchants sailed these waters freely, their dhows carrying cotton and spices to every port from Zanzibar to Malacca. Now, European interlopers demand passes and tribute from Gujarati vessels in their own waters.

Gujarat must respond. Shall the sultanate fortify its coastline and prepare to resist these foreign aggressors, or study their methods and adopt their technology to compete on equal terms?

options.text: Fortify every port: they shall not land unopposed.

modifiers.name: Coastal Bulwark
modifiers.text: Stung by the arrival of European interlopers, Gujarat has invested heavily in coastal fortifications and naval readiness to defend its shores.

options.text: Learn their methods. Build their ships. Beat them at their own game.

modifiers.name: Adopted Cannonry
modifiers.text: Rather than retreating from the European challenge, Gujarat has embraced gunpowder technology and modern shipbuilding to match its rivals at sea.

advances.name: Ghurab Warfare
advances.text: The ghurab, an oared warship armed with cannon, represents Gujarat's adaptation of Arabian naval traditions to the gunpowder age.

advances.name: Bahadur Shah's Legacy
advances.text: Sultan Bahadur Shah's defiant resistance against both the Mughal Empire and the Portuguese demonstrated Gujarat's determination to maintain its independence.

advances.name: Indigo Dye Industry
advances.text: Gujarat's indigo processing industry produces vast quantities of blue dye for both domestic textile production and export to markets across the Indian Ocean.

advances.name: Gujarati Merchant Diaspora
advances.text: Gujarati merchants have established permanent trading communities from Aden to Malacca, creating a commercial network that spans the entire Indian Ocean.

event.title: The Gujarati Merchant Diaspora
event.text:
Gujarati merchants have established permanent trading communities across the entire Indian Ocean world. In the ports of Aden and Hormuz, in the bazaars of Malacca and the Malabar Coast, Gujarati traders are recognized by their distinctive dress and their legendary commercial acumen.

These merchants carry more than goods: they carry Gujarat's culture, language, and religious traditions to distant shores. Jain and Hindu merchants from Saurashtra and Kutch have built temples in East Africa. Muslim traders from Cambay have established mosques in Southeast Asia. The Gujarati diaspora has created a commercial network that spans half the globe, connected by family ties, shared language, and mutual trust.

This network gives Gujarat an intelligence advantage and commercial reach that no army could achieve.

options.text: Our merchants are our greatest ambassadors.

advances.name: Mercantile Law
advances.text: Gujarat's legal traditions for resolving commercial disputes draw on both Islamic jurisprudence and local mercantile custom, providing a stable framework for international trade.

advances.name: Reformed Cavalry
advances.text: Gujarat's cavalry has evolved from the ghulam tradition into a professional provincial force equipped with firearms and trained in modern tactics.

advances.name: Surat Shipyards
advances.text: The dockyards of Surat have become one of the premier shipbuilding centers in the Indian Ocean, producing vessels for both domestic and foreign clients.

advances.name: Surat Entrepot
advances.text: Surat has eclipsed Cambay as Gujarat's premier port, becoming an international entrepot where European, Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants meet and trade.

advances.name: Communal Harmony
advances.text: Gujarat's tradition of multi-confessional governance, accommodating Jain, Hindu, and Muslim communities side by side, creates a stable and prosperous society.

advances.name: European Gunnery
advances.text: Surat's shipyards have incorporated European naval gunnery techniques, producing warships that combine Indian craftsmanship with European firepower.

advances.name: Mughal Textile Hub
advances.text: Under Mughal administration, Gujarat's textile industry has expanded enormously, supplying cotton cloth and silk to markets from Ottoman Turkey to Ming China.

advances.name: Surat Presidency
advances.text: Surat has become the foremost port of the Mughal Empire, a cosmopolitan city where the wealth of India meets the trade networks of the world.

advances.name: Hundi Banking Networks
advances.text: Gujarati bankers and moneylenders have developed the hundi system: a sophisticated network of bills of exchange that facilitates trade across the entire Indian Ocean.

advances.name: Fortified Cities
advances.text: Gujarat's major cities are protected by formidable walls and fortifications, a legacy of centuries of conflict between sultanate, Mughal, Maratha, and European powers.

advances.name: Revenue Reform
advances.text: Centralized tax collection and standardized administrative procedures have streamlined Gujarat's revenue system, increasing the crown's share of the region's immense wealth.

advances.name: Cotton Mechanization
advances.text:
Early mechanization of cotton processing (ginning, carding, and spinning) has begun to transform Gujarat's textile industry from artisanal craft to proto-industrial production.

Available in: Gujarat Cotton Mill

advances.name: Industrial Textiles
advances.text: Gujarat's textile industry has fully industrialized, with mechanized mills producing vast quantities of cotton cloth and fine fabrics for global markets.

advances.name: Naval Modernization
advances.text: Gujarat's navy has been rebuilt with modern steamships and iron-hulled vessels, reasserting the region's traditional command of the Arabian Sea.

advances.name: Cultural Revival
advances.text: A renewed appreciation for Gujarat's unique architectural heritage and textile traditions drives a cultural renaissance that attracts scholars and artists from across the subcontinent.

advances.name: Global Diaspora
advances.text: The Gujarati diaspora has expanded beyond the Indian Ocean to encompass the entire globe, with merchant communities in London, Zanzibar, Singapore, and beyond.

destiny.name: Gujarat United
destiny.text: With Gujarat formed and stability restored, the sultanate stands ready to pursue its national destiny. Whether by conquest or commerce, Gujarat's future shall be written in the annals of history.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: Gujarat United
event.text:
The lands of Gujarat are united under a single banner. From the salt flats of Kutch to the teak forests of the southern hills, from the ancient port of Cambay to the rising docks of Surat, this sultanate commands both the wealth of the land and the trade of the sea.

The path ahead is ours to choose. Let us build upon this foundation and forge a destiny worthy of our people.

destiny.name: Campaign into Malwa
destiny.text: The fertile plateau of Malwa, with its ancient cities of Mandu and Ujjain, beckons Gujarat's armies. Controlling this hinterland will secure the sultanate's eastern flank and provide the agricultural wealth needed to sustain further conquests.

conditions.text: Chose Sultan of Land and Sea
Own Mandu, or a subject owns it
Own Ujjain, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: The Fall of Malwa
event.text:
Our armies have marched through the Vindhya passes and planted Gujarat's banner over the ancient cities of Malwa. The fortress-capital of Mandu, perched on its great plateau, and the sacred city of Ujjain, seat of astronomers and scholars, now answer to the sultanate.

The fertile black-soil plains of Malwa will feed our armies, while its strategic position opens the road to central India. The Sultan of Land and Sea advances.

options.text: Malwa is ours. The campaign continues.

destiny.name: Conquest of the Konkan
destiny.text: The Konkan coast, stretching south from Gujarat to Goa, is dotted with wealthy ports that have fallen under foreign or rival control. Seizing Chaul and Goa will give the sultanate command of the western Indian coastline and deny these harbors to European interlopers.

conditions.text: Own Chaul, or a subject owns it
Own Goa, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50

event.title: The Konkan Secured
event.text:
The fall of Chaul and Goa has given Gujarat unbroken command of the western Indian coastline. Portuguese factories and Deccani garrisons alike have been swept aside. Our fleets now patrol from the Gulf of Kutch to the Malabar approaches without challenge.

With the Konkan coast secured, the sultan must decide how best to consolidate these gains. Shall we train our engineers in the systematic reduction of fortresses, turning Gujarat's army into the premier siege force of the subcontinent? Or shall we invest in heavy warships to project naval power across the Arabian Sea?

options.text: Train siege engineers to crack any fortress.

modifiers.name: Siege Masters
modifiers.text: Gujarat's military engineers have mastered the art of fortress reduction, training specialized sappers and deploying devastating mining techniques against enemy walls.

options.text: Build a fleet to command the Arabian Sea.

modifiers.name: Arabian Sea Command
modifiers.text: Gujarat's fleet dominates the Arabian Sea, heavy warships patrolling the trade lanes and extracting tribute from passing merchantmen.

destiny.name: Sultan Supreme
destiny.text: From the Indus to the Ganges, from Sindh to Delhi itself, the Sultan of Gujarat claims dominion over the heartland of the subcontinent. Only by holding these ancient seats of power can Gujarat's ruler truly call himself supreme.

conditions.text: Own Thatta, or a subject owns it
Own Delhi, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Army size at least 75

event.title: Sultan Supreme
event.text:
From Thatta on the Indus to Delhi on the Yamuna, the Sultan of Gujarat now rules over lands that once belonged to the great empires of the subcontinent. The ancient Sultanate of Delhi, the Sindhi ports of the Indus delta, the rich plains of Hindustan: all now acknowledge Gujarat's supremacy.

This is the apex of Gujarati power. The sultan must now decide how to govern this vast empire. Shall we establish a magnificent imperial court in the tradition of the great Sultanates, overawing our subjects with the splendor of our administration? Or shall we rule through a network of intelligence and intrigue, ensuring no rebellion can take root undetected?

options.text: Establish an imperial court of unmatched splendor.

modifiers.name: Imperial Court of Gujarat
modifiers.text: A magnificent imperial administration centered on the darbar, where the sultan receives tribute from vassal kings and dispenses justice across a vast domain.

options.text: Rule through intelligence and subtle control.

modifiers.name: Spymaster Sultan
modifiers.text: The sultan rules through an extensive intelligence network, with agents embedded in every province and court, ensuring no threat goes undetected.

destiny.name: Revival of Cambay
destiny.text: Before Gujarat can command the Indian Ocean, it must first revive the legendary prosperity of Cambay. Ensure cotton flows through the capital market, fill the treasury, and build up the port of Cambay itself.

conditions.text: Chose Gateway of the Indian Ocean
The capital

children.text: Cotton is produced in the market
Cotton is traded in the market

conditions.text: Gold at least 1000
We hold Khambat (Cambay) and it has at least 39 development

event.title: The Revival of Cambay
event.text:
The port of Cambay (Khambhat) has been restored to its legendary prosperity. Cotton bales fill the warehouses, merchants crowd the bazaars, and the sound of hammers rings from the shipyards. Gujarat's treasury overflows with the profits of commerce, and the city has grown to carry the trade.

This is only the beginning. The Indian Ocean awaits.

options.text: Our merchants shall carry Gujarat's banner to every port.

destiny.name: Gateway to Hormuz
destiny.text: The island fortress of Hormuz controls the entrance to the Persian Gulf, the richest trade route in the Indian Ocean. Gujarat's merchants have long traded there; now the sultanate must seize it outright, build a Cambay Emporium there, and establish direct control over this vital chokepoint.

conditions.text: Own Hormuz, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000
We hold Hormuz and a Cambay Emporium stands there

event.title: The Pearl of the Gulf
event.text:
The fortress-island of Hormuz, commanding the narrow strait that connects the Persian Gulf to the Indian Ocean, now flies Gujarat's banner. Every ship carrying the silks of Persia, the dates of Arabia, and the horses of the Gulf must pass under our guns.

With Hormuz secured, Gujarat controls the richest chokepoint in the Indian Ocean trade system. The sultan must decide how to leverage this position. Shall we invest in infrastructure, building new ports and warehouses to handle the flood of commerce? Or shall we empower our merchant communities abroad, turning the Gujarati diaspora into a network of commercial princes who dominate distant markets?

options.text: Build ports worthy of our new dominion.

modifiers.name: Builder of Ports
modifiers.text: Massive investment in port infrastructure across the trade network creates a web of Gujarati-built harbors that dominate Indian Ocean commerce.

options.text: Empower our merchants to rule distant markets.

modifiers.name: Merchant Princes
modifiers.text: Gujarat's merchant diaspora has evolved from trading communities into political powers, with Gujarati commercial princes controlling markets from Aden to Malacca.

destiny.name: Empire of the Indian Ocean
destiny.text: From Kilwa on the African coast to Malacca at the gateway to the South China Sea, Gujarat's commercial empire spans the entire Indian Ocean. Control of these distant ports crowns the sultanate as the undisputed master of oceanic trade.

conditions.text: Own Malacca, or a subject owns it
Own Kilwa, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Empire of the Indian Ocean
event.text:
From Kilwa on the Swahili Coast to Malacca at the gateway to the South China Sea, Gujarat's commercial empire now spans the entire Indian Ocean. Gujarati merchants sit in the counting houses of every major port. Gujarati ships dominate every sea lane. Gujarati cloth, dyes, and spices fill the markets of three continents.

No other power has achieved such commercial dominion over the world's richest ocean. The sultan must decide the character of this unprecedented empire. Shall Gujarat rule the waves as a sovereign maritime power, projecting political authority across the ocean? Or shall we perfect our role as the world's great textile producer, clothing the nations of the earth in Gujarati cotton and silk?

options.text: We shall be sovereign of the Indian Ocean.

modifiers.name: Ocean Sovereign
modifiers.text: Gujarat commands the Indian Ocean not merely as a trading power but as a political sovereign, with vassal ports and tributary states acknowledging the sultanate's maritime supremacy.

options.text: The world shall wear Gujarat's cloth.

modifiers.name: Cloth of Gold
modifiers.text: Gujarat's textile industry has achieved global dominance, with Gujarati silk and fine cloth adorning the elites of every civilization from Europe to China.

units.name: Habshi Guard
units.text: Abyssinian elite palace guards, prized for their martial prowess and unwavering loyalty to the sultan.

units.name: Ghulam Cavalry
units.text: Slave-soldier heavy cavalry whose loyalty lies entirely with the throne, forming the sultanate's mobile striking force.

units.name: Gujarati Dhow
units.text: A swift lateen-rigged trading vessel, built by Gujarat's master shipwrights for the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean.

units.name: Ghurab War Galley
units.text: An oared warship armed with cannon, designed for Arabian Sea patrol and coastal warfare.

units.name: Sipahi-e-Gujarat
units.text: Reformed provincial cavalry equipped with firearms and trained in the combined-arms tactics of the gunpowder era.

units.name: Surat Frigate
units.text: A European-influenced warship built at the Surat dockyards, combining Indian craftsmanship with modern gunnery.

units.name: Surat Merchant Cruiser
units.text: A large armed merchantman built at the Surat dockyards, designed to protect Gujarat's far-flung trade convoys across the Indian Ocean.

buildings.name: Vav Stepwell
buildings.text: Monumental stepped water wells combining sacred architecture with practical water management, a hallmark of Gujarati engineering.

buildings.name: Karkhana Workshop
buildings.text: A royal textile manufactory producing fine cloth, silk, and dyed fabrics for both domestic consumption and export.

buildings.name: Cambay Emporium
buildings.text: A grand trading house at the crossroads of Indian Ocean commerce, where Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants exchange the wealth of three continents.

buildings.name: Jama Masjid
buildings.text: A magnificent congregational mosque in the Indo-Islamic style, serving as both a center of worship and a hub of religious learning.

buildings.name: Mandvi Customs House
buildings.text: A port administration building that collects tariffs and oversees maritime commerce, ensuring orderly trade and naval recruitment.

buildings.name: Indigo Vats
buildings.text: Masonry vats beside the indigo fields, as at Sarkhej outside Ahmedabad. The cut plants are steeped and beaten, and the blue sediment is boiled and pressed into the cakes the merchants of Cambay ship across the Indian Ocean. It raises the dyes the land itself gives.

where.text: The location's raw material is Dyes

buildings.name: Hundi Banking House
buildings.text: A financial institution specializing in bills of exchange and maritime insurance, connecting Gujarat's merchants to banking networks across the Indian Ocean.

buildings.name: Gujarat Cotton Mill
buildings.text: A proto-industrial textile factory where mechanized ginning, carding, and spinning transform raw cotton into cloth at unprecedented scale.

buildings.name: Darbar-i-Khas
buildings.text: A magnificent imperial audience hall where the Sultan Supreme receives tribute from vassal kings and dispenses justice, symbol of Gujarat's dominion over the subcontinent.

buildings.name: Bandar-e-Bozorg
buildings.text: A great port complex serving as the central hub of Gujarat's Indian Ocean trade empire, with vast warehouses, shipyards, and counting houses handling the commerce of three continents.

list.name: Mahajan Panchayat
list.text: The Banya, Lohana, and Vora trader-guild courts of Cambay, Surat, Patan, and Ahmedabad. Five-elder mahajan councils adjudicated commercial disputes through customary mercantile law and underwrote the bills of exchange (hundi) that moved capital across the Indian Ocean. Both the Sultanate and the Mughal Subah of Gujarat recognized mahajan jurisdiction in commercial matters; in return the mahajans raised loans for the throne in moments of fiscal need, and the great Banya houses of Surat became the silent partners of every overseas venture from the Red Sea to the Strait of Malacca.

list.name: Khambhat Bandar
list.text: The Mutasaddi-i-Bandar's office, chief customs administration of Khambhat (Cambay), the great medieval emporium of the western Indian Ocean and the Sultanate's principal port from the fourteenth century. The bandar collected the chauth-i-bahri sea-customs on every cargo of horses from Hormuz, slaves from Zanj, spices from Malabar, and silk from China that passed through the Gulf of Khambhat. Surat inherited the apparatus after the Cambay roadstead silted up in the late sixteenth century, but the office of the Mutasaddi survived intact into the Mughal era.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Pal Sea-Protection Levy
list.text: The coastal sea-protection tax (pal or pancham) paid by Gujarati merchants and Kathiawar coastal communities to the Sultanate fleet for escort against Malabar pirates and, after 1500, against Portuguese cruisers operating from Diu and Goa. The Sultanate's standing dhow-and-ghurab navy was funded almost entirely from pal collections. Coastal villages bore the levy disproportionately and resented it bitterly, but the system built the only Indian Ocean state navy that could fight the Portuguese on roughly equal terms until the catastrophe at Diu in 1509.

list.name: Bohra Dawat-i-Hadiyah
list.text: The institutional administration of the Tayyibi Mustaali Ismaili community whose Da'i al-Mutlaq operated from Yemen and, after 1539, from Sidhpur and Surat. The Bohra mercantile diaspora ran the long-distance Indian Ocean trade in indigo, cotton textiles, and saltpetre from Cambay to Aden, Mocha, and Mombasa, with the dais collecting religious tithes and adjudicating internal affairs through their own qadis. The Sunni sultanate uneasily tolerated the network because it brought silver and Arab horses; the orthodox ulama denounced it as Shi'i deviance from the pulpits of Ahmedabad.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Begada Hill-Fort System
list.text: The chain of fortified hill-citadels (Champaner, Pavagadh, Junagadh, Idar) that Mahmud Begada secured between 1458 and 1511 as the spine of Gujarati territorial control. Each fort was held by an amir-i-qila garrisoned with ghulam cavalry and Habshi guards, and the iqta land grants supporting the garrisons were rotated to prevent the formation of hereditary fortress lordships. Champaner served briefly as the second capital; the system gave the Sultanate its remarkable resistance against Mughal armies until 1573 and remained the Mughal Subah's instrument of internal control thereafter.

list.name: Darbari Brahmin Council
list.text: The distinctive Gujarati practice of retaining Hindu accountants and advisors at the diwan-i-khalsa, drawn from the Nagar Brahmins of Vadnagar and the Audich Brahmins of north Gujarat. The Brahmin diwans kept the revenue rolls in Gujarati and Sanskrit-derived script, mediated between the Persian-speaking court and the rural Hindu cultivators, and survived dynastic transitions that swept aside their Muslim counterparts. The Mughal Subah of Gujarat formalized the practice; the same Brahmin lineages later served the Marathas and the East India Company without interruption: the institutional continuity of Hindu accountancy beneath every regime.
